name: Active Record (Ruby on Rails)
summary: The model layer of Ruby on Rails and the best-known implementation of Fowler’s Active Record pattern: each Ruby class wraps a table, each object a row, and objects load, validate and save themselves.
intro: In Active Record a model class such as `Book` maps to a table by convention, with no configuration: the class name is pluralised to find the `books` table, the primary key is an integer `id`, foreign keys are named like `author_id`, and `created_at` and `updated_at` are filled in automatically. Columns become attributes automatically: an empty `class Product < ActiveRecord::Base; end` already has accessors for every column of `products`. Objects carry both data and behaviour: `Book.find_by(title: ...)` loads one, setting `book.title` and calling `book.save` writes an `UPDATE`, and validations and callbacks run around each save. Associations (`belongs_to`, `has_many`) are declared with one line each, and migrations describe schema changes in a Ruby DSL instead of SQL.

Associations load lazily, so iterating over 10 books and reading each author runs 11 queries; the Rails guide calls this the N + 1 queries problem. `includes`, `preload` and `eager_load` load associations up front, turning those 11 queries into 2, and `strict_loading` raises an error on any lazy load that slips through. When the query interface isn’t enough, `find_by_sql` runs your own SQL and still returns model objects. Active Record supports MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL and SQLite and ships as the `activerecord` gem with every Rails release; Rails 8.1 is the current series.
strengths: Convention over configuration: a model with associations and validations can be a handful of lines
Migrations, validations, callbacks and associations integrated with the rest of Rails
Readable query interface that stays the same across MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL and SQLite
Tools against N+1 built in: `includes`, `preload`, `eager_load` and `strict_loading`
limits: Domain objects are tied to the database: persistence and business logic share one class, the opposite of the Data Mapper separation, so models tend to grow large
Lazy associations make N+1 queries easy to write unless strict loading is turned on
Built around Rails conventions; legacy schemas that break them need explicit overrides for table names and keys
Validations and callbacks run per object on `save`; fast bulk changes such as `update_all` bypass them, so the two paths can behave differently

story: David Heinemeier Hansson extracted Ruby on Rails from Basecamp, the project management tool he was building at 37signals, and released it as open source in July 2004. Its database layer took its name and design from the Active Record pattern Martin Fowler had described in Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002): an object that wraps a row in a table, encapsulates the database access and adds domain logic on that data.

Rails 1.0 arrived on 13 December 2005, 15 months after the first public release. Active Record combined convention over configuration, migrations written in Ruby and one-line association declarations. Hansson’s view, as Fowler later summed it up, was that anyone building on a relational database should know how it works: Active Record takes care of the boring parts but provides “manholes” to get down to SQL.

Active Record has shipped with every Rails release since, as the `activerecord` gem. Rails 8.0 came in November 2024 and 8.1 in October 2025, with additions over the years such as strict loading to catch N+1 queries and composite primary keys.

choices.choice: Data and database access in the same object
choices.why: Hansson’s doctrine admits this offends purists by mixing database interfacing with business logic, but argues it proved the practical way to build web apps that almost always persist their domain in a database.

If applications are configured the same way most of the time, that way should be the default. Naming conventions for tables, keys and timestamps remove most of the mapping configuration other ORMs need.
Describing changes in a Ruby DSL rather than raw SQL keeps the schema’s history in the codebase and portable across the databases Rails supports.
Rather than pretend the database isn’t there, Active Record handles routine queries and leaves `find_by_sql` and raw SQL available for the rest.
